cards.definition: A pure substance made of only one type of atom.
Two or more different types of atom chemically joined together.
Two or more substances together but not chemically joined.
More than two atoms joined together.
An early model for the structure of the atom, proposed before the nucleus was discovered.
A particle in the nucleus of an atom with a charge of +1 and a mass of 1.
A particle in the nucleus of an atom with no charge and a mass of 1.
A particle orbiting the nucleus of an atom with a charge of -1 and negligible mass.
The energy levels that electrons occupy around the nucleus; the first three hold 2, 8 and 8 electrons.
The type of substance that can be separated by physical methods such as filtration or distillation.
In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons.
Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.
Reactivity increases as you go down Group 1 — outer electron is further from the nucleus.
Reactivity decreases as you go down Group 7 — harder to gain an electron.
Group 0 elements are unreactive because they have a full outer electron shell.
The scientist who developed the periodic table by arranging elements in order of atomic mass.
Each period of the periodic table contains elements with the same number of electron shells.
Metals are usually hard, shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, sonorous, and solid at room temperature.
The reason metals are good conductors — they have free electrons that can move and carry charge.
The electrons involved in chemical reactions are those in the outer shell.
An atom with a positive or negative charge, formed by gaining or losing electrons.
A type of bonding between metals and non-metals where electrons are donated and received.
A type of bonding between two non-metals where electrons are shared.
A type of bonding between metals only, involving free electrons.
Solid, liquid and gas — the three states in which matter can exist.
The state of matter that has the most energy — particles move fastest and are furthest apart.
Covalent structures with low melting and boiling points that are non-conductors of electricity.
Structures such as diamond and graphite with very high melting and boiling points.
The element that makes both diamond and graphite — two different forms of the same element.
A mixture of metals; used because alloys are cheaper, stronger, better conductors or more corrosion resistant.
A giant covalent structure of carbon with a tetrahedral arrangement making it very hard.
A giant covalent structure of carbon made of layers that can slide over each other, making it soft.
A single layer of graphite — an extremely strong, conductive material with many potential uses.
Hollow cage-like molecules of carbon used in drug delivery, lubricants and reinforcing structures.
A long chain molecule made up of many repeating units joined together.
Ionic compounds have high melting points, dissolve in water and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.
A structure of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
The weak forces between molecules in a simple covalent structure that give it a low melting point.
In a solid, particles are closely packed in an ordered arrangement and vibrate in fixed positions.
In a liquid, particles touch but are randomly arranged and can flow past each other.
The chemicals at the start of a reaction that are used up.
The chemicals made at the end of a reaction.
The law stating that the mass of reactants always equals the mass of products in a reaction.
The mass of one atom of an element, found on the periodic table.
The total mass of one molecule, found by adding up the relative atomic masses of all its atoms.
The measurement of the amount of a substance present; 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
When a gas is produced in an open container, the recorded mass decreases as gas escapes.
The difference between the smallest and biggest result in a set of data.
A chemical equation where the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, measured in mol/dm³.
A reaction involving the addition of oxygen, or the loss of electrons (OIL RIG).
A reaction involving the loss of oxygen, or the gain of electrons (OIL RIG).
Metal oxides have a pH of 8 to 14 — they are alkaline.
A mnemonic for redox reactions: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
The type of reaction between an acid and an alkali that produces a salt and water.
The method used to separate ionic compounds by passing an electric current through them when molten or dissolved.
Produces aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
Produces copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
Acids have a pH below 7; the lower the pH, the stronger the acid.
Alkalis have a pH above 7; the higher the pH, the stronger the alkali.
A chemical reaction that gives out heat energy to the surroundings, e.g. oxidation and neutralisation.
A chemical reaction that takes in heat energy from the surroundings, e.g. thermal decomposition.
A graph that shows the energy changes during a chemical reaction, including activation energy.
Exothermic reactions are used in self-heating cans and hand warmers.
Endothermic reactions are used in sports injury packs.
An endothermic reaction where a compound breaks down when heated.
A measurement made during an experiment to identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
The minimum amount of energy needed to start a chemical reaction.
The amount of chemical energy stored in the bonds between atoms; breaking bonds requires energy, forming bonds releases energy.
A substance that lowers the activation energy of a reaction, increasing the rate without being used up.

topics.name: Rate and Extent of Chemical Change

blocks.block_name: Rate and Extent of Chemical Change (1)

cards.definition: The speed at which chemicals react, measured in g/s or cm³/s.
The chemicals that are reacting together at the start of a reaction.
The chemicals that are being made or produced during a reaction.
The variable measured during rates of reaction investigations — mass lost or volume of gas produced.
Concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts all affect the rate of a reaction.
The idea that explains how various factors affect rates of reactions — more collisions = faster reaction.
Particles must collide with sufficient energy to cause a chemical reaction to take place.
A substance that changes the rate of a reaction without being chemically changed itself.
A biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms.
Increasing surface area increases the rate of reaction by exposing more particles to collide.

blocks.block_name: Rate and Extent of Chemical Change (2)

cards.definition: A chemical reaction in which the products can react together to produce the original reactants.
The symbol used to represent a reversible reaction.
When both reactants and products are present in concentrations where no further net change occurs.
The way of predicting how a change in conditions will affect a system in equilibrium.
Concentration, temperature and pressure can all shift the position of equilibrium.
A reversible industrial process for producing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
The minimum amount of energy needed for a collision to result in a reaction.
The degree to which a reaction proceeds towards products.
Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction by increasing the frequency of collisions.
Increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction by giving particles more energy and causing more frequent, energetic collisions.
A group of fuels made from dead organisms over millions of years, e.g. coal, oil and gas.
A liquid fossil fuel found in rocks, made of a mixture of hydrocarbons.
A group of chemicals made from hydrogen and carbon only.
Hydrocarbons with all single bonds between carbon atoms; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀).
The type of bond between atoms in hydrocarbon molecules.
A molecule that has no carbon-carbon double bonds and cannot bond to any more atoms.
A way of representing molecules using chemical symbols, e.g. H₂O.
A graphical representation showing how atoms are arranged and bonded in a molecule.
Hydrocarbons with a carbon-carbon double bond; general formula CₙH₂ₙ.
The process used to separate crude oil into fractions based on different boiling points.
Fractions are used as fuels, solvents and lubricants.
The physical property that allows crude oil fractions to be separated by fractional distillation.
A measurement of how thick or runny a substance is.
Shorter chain hydrocarbons are the most flammable fractions.
The process of splitting long chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones.
Bromine water turns from brown/yellow to colourless in the presence of alkenes (unsaturated molecules).
A simple large chemical made of many repeating units joined together, e.g. polythene.
The reaction in which many small monomer molecules join together to form a polymer.
A molecule containing a carbon-carbon double bond, e.g. alkenes, which can undergo addition reactions.
A substance made of a single element or compound with nothing added to it.
A mixture that has been deliberately designed as a useful product, e.g. medicines, paints.
A technique used to separate substances — usually different colours — based on how far they travel.
The solid part of chromatography — usually paper — that does not move.
The fluid (solvent) part of chromatography that moves through the stationary phase.
The ratio of the distance moved by a compound to the distance moved by the solvent front.
Hold a lit splint at the end of a test tube — hydrogen makes a squeaky pop.
Insert a glowing splint into the gas — oxygen relights the splint.
Bubble the gas through limewater — carbon dioxide turns it cloudy/milky.
Put damp litmus paper into the gas — chlorine bleaches it white.
Makes up approximately 80% of the Earth's atmosphere.
Makes up approximately 20% of the Earth's atmosphere.
Less than 1% of the atmosphere consists of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.
The Earth is approximately 4.6 billion years old.
Mars and Venus have a similar atmosphere to Earth's early atmosphere — mostly carbon dioxide.
Earth's early atmosphere was made up of carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia.
The process that put oxygen into Earth's atmosphere, carried out by early algae.
Algae first started producing oxygen approximately 2.7 billion years ago.
Carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere by dissolving into oceans, forming fossil fuels and forming sedimentary rocks.
The group of gases trapping heat in the atmosphere and causing global warming, mainly CO₂ and methane.
The two main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide and methane.
Burning fossil fuels and cattle farming are two human activities that increase greenhouse gas levels.
Potential effects include rising temperatures, melting ice caps, rising sea levels and more extreme weather.
A toxic, colourless and odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion of fuels.
Pollutants formed at high temperatures when nitrogen in the air reacts with oxygen.
A pollutant formed when sulfur impurities in fossil fuels are burned.
Tiny particles formed by the incomplete combustion of fuels; cause global dimming and health problems.
Caused by sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolving in rainwater; damages ecosystems and buildings.
The effect of carbon particulates in the atmosphere reducing the amount of sunlight reaching Earth.
A substance introduced into the environment that has an undesired harmful effect.
Earth's natural resources are used for warmth, shelter, food and transport.
Products that are created by nature, e.g. wood, cotton.
Products that are created using chemistry, e.g. plastics, medicines.
Water that is safe for drinking — low levels of micro-organisms and dissolved salts.
The way large particulates are removed from water during treatment.
The way micro-organisms are removed from water; methods include chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light.
The process of removing salt from seawater to make it potable; uses distillation or reverse osmosis.
Wastewater produced by people that must be treated before being released back into the environment.
A rock that contains a metal compound in sufficient quantities to make extraction worthwhile.
The way of obtaining raw materials from the ground.
Using plants to absorb and accumulate metal compounds from the soil for extraction.
Using bacteria to extract metal compounds from low-grade ores.
A method of extracting pure copper using a more reactive metal such as iron.
A method of purifying copper using electricity.
A method of assessing the environmental impact of a product throughout its lifetime.
Extraction of raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal.
Three ways of decreasing the amount of natural resources consumed.
The gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reactions with its environment, e.g. rusting.
Alloys are used because they can be cheaper, stronger, better conductors or more corrosion resistant than pure metals.
A method of desalination that forces water through a membrane, leaving dissolved salts behind.
